title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Remote working has been modern trend nowadays. However, it is necessary to know what kind of abilities do the employers require for. This post uses web scraping to collect 25 recent remote tech job postings from We Work Remotely and analyzes the full job descriptions to identify which technical skills appear most often.
The goal is not just to demonstrate scraping, but to answer a practical question: if you are preparing for a remote tech career, what should you learn first?

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Data Collection
I used the rvest package in R to parse the public RSS feed from We Work Remotely’s programming jobs category.

library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)

url <- "https://weworkremotely.com/categories/remote-programming-jobs.rss"
page <- read_html(url)
items <- page %>% html_elements("item")

length(items)

[1] 25

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Data Cleaning
Each RSS <item> contains a title, region, category, publication date, and a full job description. I extracted all five fields into a tidy data frame.

titles       <- items %>% html_element("title") %>% html_text2()
regions      <- items %>% html_element("region") %>% html_text2()
categories   <- items %>% html_element("category") %>% html_text2()
dates        <- items %>% html_element("pubdate") %>% html_text2()
descriptions <- items %>% html_element("description") %>% html_text2()

jobs <- tibble(
  title       = titles,
  region      = regions,
  category    = categories,
  date        = dates,
  description = descriptions
)

glimpse(jobs)

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Analysis
I defined a list of 30 common technical skills and counted how many job descriptions mention each one. I used word-boundary regex (\\b) to avoid false matches — for example, ensuring that “Java” does not match “JavaScript”, and that “AI” does not match “email”.

skills_list <- c(
  "Python", "JavaScript", "TypeScript", "Java", "Golang",
  "React", "Vue", "Angular", "Node", "Django", "Flask",
  "SQL", "PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "MongoDB",
  "AWS", "Azure", "GCP", "Docker", "Kubernetes",
  "Git", "CI/CD", "GraphQL",
  "Machine Learning", "TensorFlow", "PyTorch",
  "HTML", "CSS", "Linux", "Bash"
)

skill_counts <- tibble(
  skill = skills_list,
  n = map_int(skills_list, function(s) {
    sum(str_detect(jobs$description,
                   regex(paste0("\\b", s, "\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE)))
  })
) |>
  filter(n > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(n))

print(skill_counts, n = 30)

  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = skill)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, size = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Most In-Demand Technical Skills in Remote Jobs",
    subtitle = "Based on 25 job postings from We Work Remotely",
    x = "Number of postings mentioning this skill",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: We Work Remotely (https://weworkremotely.com)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  expand_limits(x = max(skill_counts$n) * 1.2)




Most in-demand technical skills in remote tech jobs

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Key Findings
1. Frontend frameworks lead the pack. React appears in 10 out of 25 postings (40%) — more than any other skill. This confirms that modern remote employers expect engineers to be comfortable building interactive user interfaces.
2. Cloud and DevOps skills are the new baseline. AWS (9), CI/CD (8), Docker (7), and Kubernetes (5) together appear in over 60% of postings. Cloud infrastructure and automated deployment are common expectations for remote engineers.
3. Data and database skills are expected, not optional. MongoDB (4), PostgreSQL (2), and SQL (1) appear frequently enough to confirm that remote engineers must be comfortable working with databases, even if they are not database specialists.

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Actionable Recommendation
If you are preparing for a remote tech career, prioritize:

React — it appears in 40% of postings and is the single most requested skill.
AWS + Docker + CI/CD — this trio of cloud and DevOps skills appears across more than half of the postings.
Python — the most transferable language, useful for backend, data analysis, and machine learning roles.

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?
text:
Limitations
This analysis covers only 25 postings from a single RSS feed at one point in time. We Work Remotely is not representative of all remote work, and counting keywords in job descriptions is a rough proxy for skill demand.

title: Weekly Blog 2: What Skills Do Remote Tech Employers Actually Want?

title: Weekly Blog_Omitted variable bias
text:
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer. Run a simple regression of drownings on ice cream sales and the coefficient comes out “statistically significant.” The correlation between ice cream sales and drowning data is so strong that someone might argue a casual relationship from the data. But the two aren’t causing each other. They’re both driven by a third variable: hot weather. Hot days send people to the beach and to the ice cream truck at the same time. When that third variable is missing from the regression, the coefficient on the variable you did include quietly picks up its effect. That is omitted variable bias.
If weather belongs in the model naturally but the testing model omitted it, the regression has to stuff weather’s influence somewhere, and the only available place is the ice cream variable. And the error isn’t random noise — it’s a systematic bias that always points the same way. That’s why “significant” can be so misleading: the test says the pattern isn’t chance, but it says nothing about whether ice cream is the cause. The result looks like a causal relationship that isn’t there.


Make some data where weather drives both, and ice cream has nothing to do with drowning:

set.seed(1)
n <- 200

temp     <- rnorm(n, 80, 10)            # hot weather
icecream <- 5 * temp + rnorm(n, 0, 20)  # weather drives ice cream
drowning <- 2 * temp + rnorm(n, 0, 5)   # weather drives drownings

m_bad  <- lm(drowning ~ icecream)        # leave weather out
m_good <- lm(drowning ~ icecream + temp) # put weather back in

c(without_weather = coef(m_bad)["icecream"],
  with_weather    = coef(m_good)["icecream"])

without_weather.icecream    with_weather.icecream 
             0.344051514             -0.006568652 


Without weather, the ice cream coefficient is around 0.34 and looks significant — enough to write a headline about ice cream and drowning. Add weather and it drops to about zero. 0.34 was not ice cream’s strong effect to the drowning data, but was the weather’s effect hiding inside the ice cream variablee.



The same point can be written down. If the truth is \(y = \beta_1 x + \beta_2 z + u\) but you estimate \(y \sim x\), the coefficient converges to
\[\beta_1 + \beta_2\,\delta, \qquad \delta = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}.\]
The bias is \(\beta_2\delta\): how strongly the omitted variable moves \(y\) (\(\beta_2\)), times how tightly it moves with the variable you kept (\(\delta\)). For ice cream, both are positive, so the number comes out too big — and you can usually tell which direction the error runs just by thinking about those two signs.



The ice cream and drowning case is obvious, but when omitted variable bias happens in real life macro data, it is somehow hard to identify. For example, the bias variable inside the testing of new medicine on certain disease. In this case, it is important and necessary to apply panel data method or use proxy variables.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
Tech hiring has always been competitive, but the skills employers ask for shift constantly. With hundreds of languages, frameworks, and tools competing for attention, it is hard to know where to focus your learning.
This analysis scrapes job postings from three independent sources to answer a simple question:
Which technical skills appear most frequently in tech job postings?
The answer turns out to be surprisingly consistent across platforms.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
Tech hiring has always been competitive, but the skills employers ask for shift constantly. With hundreds of languages, frameworks, and tools competing for attention, it is hard to know where to focus your learning.
This analysis scrapes job postings from three independent sources to answer a simple question:
Which technical skills appear most frequently in tech job postings?
The answer turns out to be surprisingly consistent across platforms.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
Where the Data Comes From
I collected job postings from three different platforms, each representing a different slice of the tech hiring market:








Source
What it covers
Postings




RemoteOK
A curated remote-first job board with structured skill tags
99


We Work Remotely
A remote-only job board with detailed descriptions
25


Hacker News “Who is Hiring?”
Global startup and tech hiring, updated monthly
245



Together these sources cover a wide range of employers: from remote-first startups to established tech companies and traditional firms hiring across onsite, hybrid, and remote arrangements.
Three sources are better than one. Each platform attracts a different kind of employer, so combining them reduces the risk of drawing conclusions from a single, biased sample.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
The Skills That Keep Appearing
The clearest pattern across all three datasets is the dominance of Python. It appears in 69 of the 245 Hacker News postings (28%), and it ranks among the top skills on the other two platforms as well.
Let’s look at each source in turn.

We Work Remotely: 25 Remote Tech Postings



Skills in demand on We Work Remotely


React leads the pack, appearing in 40% of postings, followed closely by AWS and CI/CD. The pattern here points to a cloud-native, frontend-heavy skill set — exactly what you would expect from a remote-only job board.


RemoteOK: 99 Remote-First Postings



Skills in demand on RemoteOK


RemoteOK’s tag data tells a different story. Go and system administration dominate, reflecting a user base of infrastructure engineers and DevOps specialists. Backend skills are more prominent here than on the other platforms.


Hacker News: 245 Global Tech Postings



Skills in demand on Hacker News


The Hacker News sample is the largest and most diverse. Python leads with 69 mentions (28%), followed by TypeScript and React. This is the startup-heavy, full-stack profile — engineers who are expected to work across the entire product.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
How the Three Platforms Compare
The most interesting finding is not what the platforms agree on, but where they differ.








Platform
Most distinctive skill
Likely reason




We Work Remotely
React (40% of postings)
Curated board attracts design-forward companies


RemoteOK
Go / sys admin
User base of infrastructure engineers


Hacker News
Python (28% of postings)
Startup-heavy community, full-stack roles




The takeaway: There is no single “tech job market.” Different platforms serve different segments, and the skills that matter depend on which segment you are targeting.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
section: What This Means If You’re Learning
text:
What This Means If You’re Learning
If you are preparing for a career in tech — or planning what to study next — the data suggests a clear priority order:
1. Learn Python first. It is the only language that appears near the top of every platform. It works for backend engineering, data analysis, automation, and increasingly for AI.
2. Add React. Frontend skills are not optional. Even backend-leaning roles increasingly expect familiarity with a modern JavaScript framework.
3. Build cloud and DevOps literacy. AWS, Docker, and CI/CD appear together so often that they are effectively a single requirement. You do not need to be a specialist, but you do need to be comfortable.
4. Learn one database well. PostgreSQL is the safest choice, but MongoDB is also common. The specific choice matters less than having real experience with schema design and queries.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
section: What This Analysis Cannot Tell You
text:
What This Analysis Cannot Tell You
A few honest limitations:

It is a snapshot. The data was collected in September 2026 and reflects one moment in a fast-moving market.
Job postings are not hires. Employers list many skills they never actually test for. Advertised demand is a rough proxy for real demand.
Keyword counting is imprecise. A posting that mentions “Python” once counts the same as one that mentions it ten times.
Not all postings are remote. The Hacker News sample includes onsite and hybrid roles. This makes the findings broader, but less specific to remote-only hiring.

These limitations do not undermine the findings — the patterns are strong enough to be meaningful — but they are worth keeping in mind.

title: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
Conclusion
Across three independent data sources and nearly 400 job postings, the same skills keep appearing: Python, React, AWS, Docker, and CI/CD.
The specific mix varies by platform, but the core toolkit is remarkably consistent. For anyone preparing for a career in tech, the path is clear: start with Python, add frontend and cloud skills, and build real projects that demonstrate you can ship.
The data does not predict the future. But it does describe the present — and the present is a good place to start.

Data sources: RemoteOK, We Work Remotely, and Hacker News. All scraping was done ethically using public RSS feeds, APIs, and HTML pages.
